title: Works of mercy for the body
word: Works of mercy for the body
hook: feed, give drink, clothe, shelter, visit the sick and prisoners, bury the dead
tomorrow: works of mercy for the soul

segments.voice: Yesterday, lust and chastity: David on the roof, and the whole person. Your line was people, not things. Whose whole life did you give back to them? Day one thousand two hundred eight.

The table is set for a feast. A man named Tobit is about to eat, and he sends his son out to find a poor man to share the meal. The son comes back with news instead: a man of their people has been killed, and his body is lying in the marketplace. Tobit gets up before he has tasted anything. He goes out, carries the body to a room, and waits for sunset so he can bury it. His neighbors laugh at him. Burying the dead has already got him into trouble with the king. He does it anyway. His dinner, the book says, he ate in sorrow. Today: works of mercy for the body.

Tobit's book sits in the Bibles of Catholic and Orthodox Christians; Protestant Bibles that print it place it among the books called the Apocrypha. Either way, tradition says his story gave Christians one item on an old list: the works of mercy for the body. The rest of the list comes straight from Jesus. In Matthew's Gospel he tells a story of the end of all things. The nations are gathered, and the king says to some of them, in the King James words: "For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in: Naked, and ye clothed me: I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me." Food, drink, shelter, clothes, the sick, the prisoner. Add Tobit's burial, and that's the list the tradition hands on. Then the story turns. The people the king praises don't know what he's talking about. They ask, "Lord, when saw we thee an hungred, and fed thee?" They never noticed. They were just feeding people. And the king answers: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." That's the hinge. In this story, the hungry stranger and Christ are somehow the same face. So these works aren't charity from a distance. They are hands: a plate, a cup, a coat, a chair beside a hospital bed, a visit through a glass window, a shovel at a grave. Some Christians trace hospitals, soup kitchens and prison visiting back to these verses. But the works can stay small: one meal brought to one neighbor.
screen: `I WAS AN HUNGRED, AND YE GAVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one today. Settle, and breathe. Let the king's list pass by, one need at a time. Someone hungry. Someone thirsty. Someone who needs a coat, or a place to stay. Someone sick. Someone locked away, in a prison or a lonely room. Someone grieving a death. Let one name or one face rise up. Then choose one thing your hands can do for them today, however small: a meal, a call, a visit, a bag of clothes. If you pray, you can hold that person before God. The bell holds the time.
Works of mercy for the body. Feed the hungry, give drink, clothe, shelter, visit the sick and prisoners, bury the dead.
screen: `WORKS OF MERCY FOR THE BODY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: mercy with hands. Today, do the one work you chose, with your own hands, even if nobody notices, as the people in the story didn't. Day one thousand two hundred eight.

howItsDone: Christians practice the works of mercy for the body, often called the corporal works of mercy, through food banks, shelters, hospital and prison visiting, and funeral ministries, and in ordinary help to neighbors; the list comes from Matthew 25 with burial of the dead from Tobit.

notes: Tobit 2:1–8 paraphrased (the feast at Pentecost, the son sent to find a poor man, the strangled man in the marketplace, burial after sunset, neighbors' mockery, eating 'in sorrow'). Confirm details against the Douay-Rheims/KJV Apocrypha.
Canon statement: Catholic and Orthodox include Tobit; Protestant churches 'usually' place it in the Apocrypha. Confirm.
'that's the list the churches teach' and 'hospitals, soup kitchens and prison visits have grown from these verses' are general historical statements without a cited source; confirm or cut.
The trapdoor's third floor gives a count ('six works ... with burial added') that the cited text (Matthew 25:35–36) supports; the spoken script avoids the count. Confirm.
'stranger, and ye took me in' is rendered in the list as shelter; the traditional list says 'shelter the homeless' or 'harbor the stranger'. Confirm.
Original: ἔλεος; the Kyrie eleison connection (ἐλέησον from ἐλεέω) is close but not the same form. Confirm the note.
